extra.message: POST / passes attacker-controlled username and password through Passport into this concatenated SQL query. A username such as ' OR 1=1 # comments out the password condition and authenticates as the first returned user without knowing their password.

GET /error-based-sqli and GET /idor pass req.query.id into findUserById. The value is concatenated directly into SELECT * FROM users WHERE id without validation or escaping. Authenticated users can inject SQL expressions and UNION queries to extract database contents.

searchByName interpolates username into a LIKE expression. Input reaches this query from /blind-sqli, /xss-exercise, /blind-sqli-blacklist, /reflected-xss, and parsed XML at /xxe. The case-sensitive SQL blacklist permits uppercase SQL operators. /second-order-sqli also queries a previously registered or updated username, enabling second-order injection. These flows allow authenticated attackers to alter predicates and extract database data.

POST /change-password accepts JSON objects as req.body.id and passes them unchanged into a mysql placeholder. Sending {"password":"chosen","id":{"id":1}} produces WHERE id=`id` = 1, which matches every non-null user ID and changes all passwords. The profile update at line 29 similarly accepts an object through query parameter id[id]=1. The application does not validate scalar types; mysql placeholders expand objects into SQL assignments, as documented in the [mysql API](https://github.com/mysqljs/mysql/tree/v2.17.1#escaping-query-values).

POST /command-injection passes req.body.ip into pingMe, which appends it to 'ping -c 3 ' and executes the result through child_process.exec. Shell metacharacters are unrestricted, allowing an authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands with the server process's privileges.

GET /arbitrary-file-retrieval passes req.query.filename into path.join(__dirname, filename) and fs.readFile without checking the resulting path. Parent-directory segments escape utils, allowing authenticated users to read arbitrary accessible files. File contents are returned in the rendered response.

POST /xxe supplies req.body.search to libxml.parseXmlString with noent:true, enabling entity substitution without rejecting external entities. An attacker can declare a SYSTEM entity referencing file:///etc/passwd inside a user element. The expanded text is incorporated into the search response, exposing files readable by the server.

extra.message: GET /deserialization passes the unsigned, attacker-controlled user cookie here. Base64 decoding provides no integrity protection, and serialize.unserialize processes function-bearing values. An authenticated attacker can submit a _$$ND_FUNC$$_ value containing an immediately invoked function to execute arbitrary server-side JavaScript. Function evaluation is explicit in the [serializer source](https://github.com/luin/serialize/blob/master/lib/serialize.js).

GET /idor retrieves and renders the account selected by req.query.id without checking ownership against req.user.id. Changing the numeric ID exposes another user's name, email, phone, and username. GET /error-based-sqli repeats this unauthorized lookup at line 28. Route middleware only verifies that the requester is logged in.

extra.message: The shared header renders database-backed fullName using unescaped EJS output. Registration and profile updates store fullname without HTML sanitization. HTML event handlers or script elements therefore execute whenever the affected user views an authenticated page. The same raw output occurs at line 42 and views/navigation.ejs:17. The unauthorized profile-update endpoints let an attacker plant this payload in another user's account.

Stored profile fields are concatenated into HTML table cells after a case-sensitive blacklist check instead of output encoding. A fullname such as bypasses the lowercase patterns. Search pages render the generated table using unescaped EJS output, executing the stored payload in other users' browsers when they search for the malicious account.

POST /reflected-xss and /blind-sqli-blacklist reflect unmatched req.body.username values directly into HTML. The SQL blacklist does not block a payload such as <script>alert(1)</script>. Both templates render htmlResponse without escaping, allowing attacker-supplied markup to execute in the requesting user's browser.

POST /blind-sqli and /xss-exercise place an unmatched username into HTML after custom_sanitizer_regex. That sanitizer removes only the first regex match. Two consecutive elements leave the second element intact. The resulting htmlResponse is rendered unescaped, enabling reflected XSS.

getUrlVars reads the default parameter from document.location.href. The shared header URI-decodes it and passes it directly to document.write. A crafted URL containing an encoded value breaks out of the language selector and executes JavaScript when an authenticated user visits the link.

POST /xxe extracts text from the attacker-supplied user element and concatenates unmatched values into HTML without encoding. XML such as <user><script>alert(1)</script></user> becomes executable markup in res.send(htmlResponse). The normal client also inserts the response through jQuery.html at views/xxe.ejs:100.

File-read errors are concatenated into HTML and rendered unescaped by /arbitrary-file-retrieval. A nonexistent filename containing is included in the filesystem error and becomes executable response markup. The same unsafe error rendering occurs for command errors at lines 136-137 and regex errors at lines 169-170; a malformed search regex containing HTML is reflected through its SyntaxError.

POST /regex-injection inserts req.body.search directly into the regex intended to restrict results to public log entries. The value )|(.* closes the original group and adds an unrestricted alternative, matching private entries too. Matching lines are returned verbatim, exposing the private login/logout records and SSN fields in utils/customLogs.txt.

cwe: CWE-730: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements within a Regular Expression

extra.message: searchLogs synchronously tests an attacker-controlled regular expression against every log line on the Node.js event loop. A search value such as )|((.*)*)Z|( introduces nested repetition with a failing suffix. Matching the existing private log lines can require exponential backtracking, allowing an authenticated request to block processing for all users.

Registration writes user.password directly into the password column without hashing. Password changes likewise store the supplied value at line 70, and authentication compares the original password directly at line 15. Database disclosure therefore exposes immediately usable passwords; the imported SHA-512 helper is not used in these flows.

extra.message: Password changes and profile updates rely solely on cookie authentication. Neither app middleware nor handlers validate a CSRF token or Origin/Referer, and their forms contain no token. Browser-submittable URL-encoded POST requests can therefore change account data when the victim's session cookie accompanies the request. The installed csurf package is never activated, and the session configuration sets no explicit SameSite policy.

Successful authentication calls req.logIn without regenerating the existing Express session. The declared Passport 0.4.x implementation attaches authentication state to that session without rotating its ID, as shown in its [session manager](https://github.com/jaredhanson/passport/blob/v0.4.0/lib/sessionmanager.js). An attacker who plants a known valid anonymous session cookie in a victim's browser can reuse it after the victim logs in.

Logout only deletes connect.sid in the browser and navigates to /. No server logout endpoint calls req.logout or destroys the stored session. A previously copied session cookie therefore remains authenticated and can be replayed after the user has logged out.

The active session middleware uses the hardcoded signing secret 'secrettobechanged' with no deployment-specific override. Anyone with the source can generate valid signatures for chosen session IDs, defeating the cookie signature's integrity protection. Access to an authenticated server-side session is still required to impersonate its owner.

cwe: CWE-321: Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key

extra.message: The authentication session cookie explicitly sets httpOnly:false. JavaScript can read connect.sid through document.cookie, allowing the application's confirmed XSS vulnerabilities to steal reusable authenticated session cookies.

cwe: CWE-1004: Sensitive Cookie Without HttpOnly Flag

extra.message: The authentication session cookie explicitly sets secure:false, permitting transmission over unencrypted HTTP. The bundled entry point also creates an HTTP server. A network observer on an HTTP connection can capture the session cookie and replay it to impersonate the user.

cwe: CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without Secure Attribute

extra.message: The public login route invokes authentication without rate limiting, backoff, or account lockout. The Passport strategy and controller also maintain no failed-attempt counters. Attackers can repeatedly submit password guesses against an account without an application-enforced limit.
